<div class="page-shell">

<header class="masthead">
  <div class="eyebrow">WebR practical</div>
  <h1>Interaction terms in regression</h1>
  <p>Fit models where the effect of one predictor depends on another: first with a binary group, then with a polytomous (multi-level) group, and finally with two continuous predictors.</p>
</header>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Overview</h2>

An additive multiple regression assumes each predictor has the <strong>same effect at every level of the other predictors</strong>:

```r
lm(outcome ~ predictor_1 + predictor_2, data = my_data)
```

An <strong>interaction</strong> relaxes that assumption. It lets the slope of one predictor change with the value of another:

```r
lm(outcome ~ predictor_1 + predictor_2 + predictor_1:predictor_2, data = my_data)
```

The shorthand <code>predictor_1 * predictor_2</code> expands to exactly the same three terms.

In this practical you will:

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li>Compare an additive model (parallel lines) to an interaction model (each group gets its own slope) with a <strong>binary</strong> group variable.</li>
  <li>Extend the same idea to a <strong>polytomous</strong> (3-level) categorical variable.</li>
  <li>Interpret an interaction between <strong>two continuous</strong> predictors, where the slope changes smoothly instead of by group.</li>
</ul>

After answering the questions, <strong>your completion code will be revealed.</strong>

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 1</div>
  <p>Which R formula fits an interaction between <code>bmi</code> and <code>meds</code> when predicting <code>sysbp</code>?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="a"><code>lm(sysbp ~ bmi + meds, data = bp)</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="b"><code>lm(sysbp ~ bmi - meds, data = bp)</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="c"><code>lm(sysbp ~ bmi * meds, data = bp)</code></label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. bmi * meds expands to bmi + meds + bmi:meds, which includes the interaction term." data-incorrect="Not quite. A plus sign gives an additive model. The * (or an explicit bmi:meds term) adds the interaction."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 1: binary group. Does BP medication change the BMI&ndash;blood pressure relationship?</h2>

We will use a mock dataset of 60 adults. The variables are:

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><code>bmi</code>: body mass index (kg/m&sup2;).</li>
  <li><code>meds</code>: <code>"noMeds"</code> or <code>"onMeds"</code> (blood pressure medication).</li>
  <li><code>sysbp</code>: systolic blood pressure (mmHg).</li>
</ul>

The question is not just "does BMI predict blood pressure?" but: <strong>is the BMI slope different for people on medication?</strong>

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: create the data</h3>

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)

set.seed(42)
n <- 60
bmi <- round(runif(n, 20, 40), 1)
meds <- rep(c("noMeds", "onMeds"), each = n / 2)
sysbp <- 88 + 1.7 * bmi +
  ifelse(meds == "onMeds", 57 - 1.0 * bmi, 0) +
  rnorm(n, 0, 4)

bp <- data.frame(bmi, meds = factor(meds), sysbp = round(sysbp, 1))
head(bp)
```

</div>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: plot each group with its own fitted line</h3>

```{webr-r}
ggplot(bp, aes(x = bmi, y = sysbp, color = meds)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#b83b5e", "#00565e")) +
  labs(x = "BMI", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", color = "Medication") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 2</div>
  <p>In the plot, the two group lines are clearly <strong>not parallel</strong>: the on-meds line starts higher but rises more slowly. What does that suggest?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="a">An additive model is sufficient, since both lines slope upward.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="b">The BMI slope depends on medication status, so an interaction term is worth fitting.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="c">BMI and blood pressure are unrelated.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Non-parallel group lines are the visual signature of an interaction." data-incorrect="Not quite. An additive model forces the two lines to be parallel. When the slopes clearly differ, the model needs an interaction term."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Additive first: parallel lines</h2>

Before fitting the interaction, fit the additive model. It gives both groups the <strong>same BMI slope</strong> and differs only in intercept.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fit the additive model</h3>

```{webr-r}
mod_additive <- lm(sysbp ~ bmi + meds, data = bp)
summary(mod_additive)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 3</div>
  <p>In the additive model, the <code>bmi</code> slope is about <code>+1.26</code>. Who does this slope apply to?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="a">Both groups: the additive model assumes one shared BMI slope.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="b">Only the noMeds group, since it is the reference level.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="c">Only the onMeds group, since it appears in the output.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Without an interaction, the model fits one BMI slope for everyone; the groups differ only in intercept." data-incorrect="Not quite. In an additive model the slope is shared: the medsonMeds coefficient only shifts the line up or down."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Now the interaction model</h2>

Fill in the blank to add the interaction term, then run the cell.

<div class="formula-panel">

$$
\widehat{\text{sysbp}} = b_0 + b_1 \times \text{bmi} + b_2 \times \text{onMeds} + b_3 \times (\text{bmi} \times \text{onMeds})
$$

<p>Here <code>onMeds</code> is 1 for people on medication and 0 for the reference group (<code>noMeds</code>).</p>

</div>

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: exercise, fill in the blank</h3>

```{webr-r}
mod_interact <- lm(sysbp ~ bmi + meds + ____, data = bp)
summary(mod_interact)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

```r
mod_interact <- lm(sysbp ~ bmi + meds + bmi:meds, data = bp)
```

Or equivalently `lm(sysbp ~ bmi * meds, data = bp)`.

</details>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Read the output as a slopes-by-group table</h2>

Rounded to two decimals, the interaction model output is:

```r
              Estimate
(Intercept)      83.08
bmi               1.84
medsonMeds       61.62
bmi:medsonMeds   -1.10
```

The most reliable way to read this is to rebuild each group's own line:

<table class="slope-table">
<tr><th>Group</th><th>Intercept</th><th>BMI slope</th></tr>
<tr><td>noMeds (reference)</td><td>83.08</td><td>1.84</td></tr>
<tr><td>onMeds</td><td>83.08 + 61.62 = 144.70</td><td>1.84 + (&minus;1.10) = 0.74</td></tr>
</table>

The reference group's slope is the plain <code>bmi</code> row alone. The non-reference group's slope is the <code>bmi</code> row <strong>plus the interaction row</strong>.

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 4</div>
  <p>What is the BMI slope for people <strong>on medication</strong>?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="a"><code>1.84</code>, straight from the bmi row.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="b"><code>1.84 + (-1.10) = 0.74</code>, the bmi row plus the interaction row.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="c"><code>-1.10</code>, straight from the interaction row.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The interaction coefficient is the change in slope, not the slope itself." data-incorrect="Not quite. The interaction row tells you how much the on-meds slope differs from the reference slope; add it to the bmi coefficient."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 5</div>
  <p>Using the group table, what is the predicted systolic BP for someone <strong>on medication</strong> with BMI = 30?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="a"><code>83.08 + 1.84 * 30 = 138.28</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="b"><code>144.70 + 1.84 * 30 = 199.90</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="c"><code>144.70 + 0.74 * 30 = 166.90</code></label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Use the on-meds intercept and the on-meds slope." data-incorrect="Not quite. For an on-meds person, use both the on-meds intercept (144.70) and the on-meds slope (0.74)."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 6</div>
  <p>What does the <code>medsonMeds</code> coefficient (<code>+61.62</code>) represent in the interaction model?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="a">The gap between the two lines at BMI = 0 (the difference in intercepts).</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="b">The gap between the two lines at every BMI.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="c">The BMI slope for the on-meds group.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Once the slopes differ, the gap between the lines changes with BMI; 61.62 is the gap only at BMI = 0." data-incorrect="Not quite. In an additive model the gap is constant, but with an interaction the gap changes along x; the coefficient gives the gap at BMI = 0."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 2: polytomous group. Three smoking categories</h2>

The same machinery works when the categorical variable has <strong>more than two levels</strong>. We will model lung function (FEV1, in mL) against age for three smoking groups: <code>never</code> (the reference), <code>former</code>, and <code>current</code>.

With 3 levels, R creates <strong>2 dummy variables</strong> and therefore <strong>2 interaction terms</strong>: one for each non-reference level. Each one says how that group's age slope differs from the never-smokers' slope.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: create the data and fit the model</h3>

```{webr-r}
set.seed(7)
n2 <- 90
age <- round(runif(n2, 30, 70))
smoking <- rep(c("never", "former", "current"), each = 30)
fev <- 5200 - 20 * age +
  ifelse(smoking == "former", -200 - 10 * age,
    ifelse(smoking == "current", -300 - 25 * age, 0)) +
  rnorm(n2, 0, 150)

lung <- data.frame(
  age,
  smoking = factor(smoking, levels = c("never", "former", "current")),
  fev = round(fev)
)

ggplot(lung, aes(x = age, y = fev, color = smoking)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#287a4d", "#f5a623", "#b83b5e")) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "FEV1 (mL)", color = "Smoking") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

mod_lung <- lm(fev ~ age * smoking, data = lung)
summary(mod_lung)
```

</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>One row per level: the slopes-by-group table again</h2>

Rounded, the output is:

```r
                   Estimate
(Intercept)          5230.7
age                   -19.9
smokingformer        -280.8
smokingcurrent       -390.3
age:smokingformer      -9.3
age:smokingcurrent    -22.9
```

Exactly as with the binary case, each non-reference level gets its slope by <strong>adding its own interaction row</strong> to the reference slope:

<table class="slope-table">
<tr><th>Group</th><th>Intercept</th><th>Age slope (mL/year)</th></tr>
<tr><td>never (reference)</td><td>5230.7</td><td>&minus;19.9</td></tr>
<tr><td>former</td><td>5230.7 &minus; 280.8 = 4949.9</td><td>&minus;19.9 + (&minus;9.3) = &minus;29.2</td></tr>
<tr><td>current</td><td>5230.7 &minus; 390.3 = 4840.4</td><td>&minus;19.9 + (&minus;22.9) = &minus;42.8</td></tr>
</table>

Note that each interaction term compares that level to the <strong>reference</strong> group, not to the other non-reference level.

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 7</div>
  <p>If a categorical variable has 4 levels, how many interaction terms will <code>age * group</code> produce?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="a">4, one per level.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="b">3, one per non-reference level.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="c">1, because there is only one categorical variable.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The reference level is absorbed into the base coefficients, so k levels give k - 1 dummies and k - 1 interaction terms." data-incorrect="Not quite. A k-level factor becomes k - 1 dummy variables, and each dummy gets its own interaction term."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 8</div>
  <p>What is the age slope for <strong>current</strong> smokers?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="a"><code>-19.9 + (-22.9) = -42.8</code> mL/year</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="b"><code>-22.9</code> mL/year, from the age:smokingcurrent row alone</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="c"><code>-19.9 + (-9.3) + (-22.9) = -52.1</code> mL/year, adding both interaction rows</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Add only the current-smoker interaction row to the reference slope; the former-smoker row is irrelevant here." data-incorrect="Not quite. Each group's slope is the reference slope plus that group's own interaction row only."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 9</div>
  <p>What does the <code>age:smokingformer</code> coefficient (<code>-9.3</code>) itself mean?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="a">Former smokers lose 9.3 mL of FEV1 per year.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="b">Former smokers have 9.3 mL less FEV1 than current smokers at every age.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="c">Former smokers' FEV1 declines 9.3 mL/year faster than never-smokers' does.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Interaction coefficients are differences in slope relative to the reference group." data-incorrect="Not quite. -9.3 is not a slope or a gap: it is how much the former-smoker slope differs from the never-smoker slope."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 3: two continuous predictors</h2>

When both interacting variables are continuous, there are no groups and no group lines. The interpretation is the same idea taken to its limit: <strong>the slope of one predictor changes smoothly with the value of the other</strong>.

We will model systolic BP from daily sodium intake (grams/day) and age:

<div class="formula-panel">

$$
\widehat{\text{sysbp}} = b_0 + b_1 \times \text{sodium} + b_2 \times \text{age} + b_3 \times (\text{sodium} \times \text{age})
$$

<p>The slope of sodium at a given age is \(b_1 + b_3 \times \text{age}\). So \(b_1\) is the sodium slope <strong>when age = 0</strong>, and \(b_3\) is how much that slope changes per year of age.</p>

</div>

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: create the data and fit the model</h3>

```{webr-r}
set.seed(99)
n3 <- 80
sodium <- round(runif(n3, 1.5, 5), 1)
age <- round(runif(n3, 25, 75))
sysbp <- 95 + 2 * sodium + 0.3 * age +
  0.10 * sodium * age + rnorm(n3, 0, 5)

salt <- data.frame(sodium, age, sysbp = round(sysbp, 1))

mod_salt <- lm(sysbp ~ sodium * age, data = salt)
summary(mod_salt)
```

</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>A slope-at-a-value table</h2>

Rounded, the output is:

```r
             Estimate
(Intercept)     96.62
sodium           0.96
age              0.31
sodium:age       0.11
```

With a continuous "other" variable, there is no reference group. Instead of one row per level, we make one row per <strong>chosen value</strong> of age. The sodium slope at each age is <code>0.96 + 0.11 &times; age</code>:

<table class="slope-table">
<tr><th>At age&hellip;</th><th>Sodium slope (mmHg per g/day)</th></tr>
<tr><td>30</td><td>0.96 + 0.11 &times; 30 = 4.26</td></tr>
<tr><td>50</td><td>0.96 + 0.11 &times; 50 = 6.46</td></tr>
<tr><td>70</td><td>0.96 + 0.11 &times; 70 = 8.66</td></tr>
</table>

The binary and polytomous tables were special cases of this: the "chosen values" were just 0 and 1 on the dummy variables. Here the slope keeps changing at every value of age.

</section>

<div class="callout warning">

<p><strong>Careful with the main effects.</strong> In this model, <code>0.96</code> is the sodium slope at <strong>age = 0</strong>, which is far outside the data (ages run 25 to 75). It is a mathematical anchor point, not a slope for any real person. This is why analysts sometimes <em>center</em> continuous variables before fitting interactions, so the main effects describe a typical person instead.</p>

</div>
